sections.heading: What Linux is
text: Linux is an operating system: the core software that runs a computer, the same job Windows and macOS do on a laptop. It runs most of the world's web servers, nearly all cloud machines and supercomputers, every Android phone, and countless routers, cameras and other devices.

In cybersecurity you will spend a lot of time on Linux machines, and often they have no desktop or mouse at all. You control them by typing. That's what this course teaches, one small mission at a time.

sections.heading: The terminal and the shell
text: The panel on the right is a terminal: a window where you type instead of clicking. Inside it runs a program called the shell. The shell reads what you type, runs it when you press Enter, prints the result, and then waits for the next instruction.
Every instruction is called a command. Typing a command and pressing Enter is how you do everything in Linux: read files, move around, search, change settings.

sections.heading: Reading the prompt
text: Before each command the shell prints a prompt to show it's ready. Yours looks like `user@cybercodex:~$`. Every part means something:
points: `user` is your username: who you are logged in as.
`cybercodex` is the hostname: the name of the machine you're on. Useful when you're connected to several machines at once.
`~` is where you are right now. `~` is short for your home directory, your personal folder. You'll see this change as you move around.
`$` means the shell is ready for a command from a normal user. Administrators (the `root` user) see `#` instead.
You never type the prompt. Type only what comes after the `$`.

sections.heading: Commands and arguments
text: A command line is split into words at the spaces. The first word is the command: the program you want to run. Every word after it is an argument: extra information you hand to that program, such as which file to work on.
`echo` is the simplest command there is. It prints its arguments back to you. Try it in your own terminal too.

sections.heading: In Linux, almost everything is a file
text: This is the most important idea in Linux. Your documents are files, but so are the system's settings, its logs, the programs themselves, and even hardware like disks and keyboards, which appear as special files. Files are organised into directories, which is Linux's word for folders.

Because nearly everything is a file, the most basic skill on any Linux machine is reading files. Learn to read files and you can inspect almost anything: how a server is configured, what happened in a log, what a note says.

sections.heading: Reading a file with cat
text: `cat` prints everything inside a file onto your screen. You give it the filename as its argument: `cat notes.txt`. The name comes from concatenate, meaning join together: give it several files and it prints them one after another.

`cat` only reads. It never changes, moves or deletes the file, so you can run it as often as you like. If you mistype the name, Linux tells you the file doesn't exist. Names must match exactly, including the extension (`.txt`) and capital letters.

sections.heading: Linux is built for many users
text: From the start, Linux was designed for many people sharing one machine. Every person (and many background services) gets their own user account, with their own home directory and their own files. Linux keeps track of which account runs every single command and uses that to decide what it's allowed to touch.

One account is special: `root`, the administrator, who can do anything. Security work revolves around this. Defenders keep normal users away from things they shouldn't touch; attackers try to become `root`.

sections.heading: Who am I? whoami
text: When you land on an unfamiliar machine, the first question is always: which account am I using? `whoami` answers it by printing your username. It takes no arguments.

sections.heading: The numbers behind the names: id
text: Names are for humans. Internally, Linux identifies every user by a number called the UID (user ID), and every group by a GID (group ID). `id` prints all of them at once.
points: `uid=1000(user)`: your user ID is 1000 and its name is `user`. Normal accounts usually start at 1000.
`gid=1000(user)`: your main group. A group is a named set of users who can be given shared access to files.
`groups=...`: every group you belong to. More groups usually means more access.
The UID of `root` is always 0. Seeing `uid=0` means you have full control of the machine.

To read a file inside a folder, join the folder name and the filename with a `/`. `letters/user.txt` means the file `user.txt` inside the folder `letters`.

sections.heading: The filesystem is a tree
text: All files on a Linux machine sit in one big tree of directories. The very top of the tree is called the root directory and is written as a single `/`. Every other directory hangs somewhere below it. (Don't confuse the root directory `/` with the `root` user. Same word, different things.)
There's only one tree. Unlike Windows, there's no `C:` or `D:` drive: extra disks are attached somewhere inside the same tree.

sections.heading: The standard directories
text: Most Linux systems use the same layout, so once you know it you can find your way around any machine:
points: `/home`: users' personal directories. Yours is `/home/user`.
`/etc`: system settings, mostly plain text files you can read.
`/var`: data that changes while the system runs. Logs are in `/var/log`.
`/tmp`: temporary files that anyone can create and that may be wiped.
`/opt`: optional, add-on software. Missions often hide things in `/opt/academy`.

sections.heading: Paths: the address of a file
text: You describe where something is in the tree with a path: the directories to walk through from the top, separated by `/`. `/home/user/projects/alpha/plan.txt` reads as: start at the root `/`, go into `home`, then `user`, then `projects`, then `alpha`, and there is `plan.txt`.

sections.heading: Where am I? pwd
text: Your shell is always standing in one directory, called the working directory (or current directory). `pwd` (print working directory) prints its full path.

This matters because when you type a name without a leading `/`, like `cat plan.txt`, Linux looks for it in your working directory. Two directories can each contain a `plan.txt`; which one you read depends on where you're standing. The prompt shows your location too, with `~` standing for `/home/user`.

sections.heading: Listing a directory
text: `ls` (list) shows the names of the files and directories inside a directory. With no argument it lists your working directory; give it a path to list somewhere else. It's how you look around before doing anything.

sections.heading: Options change how a command behaves
text: Most commands accept options (also called flags): arguments that start with a dash and switch a feature on. `ls -a` means: list, and include everything. `ls -l` means: list in the long format, with details.
You can combine single-letter options behind one dash: `ls -la` is the same as `ls -l -a`. Options usually go before any filenames.

sections.heading: Hidden files
text: By convention, any file or directory whose name starts with a dot (`.settings`, `.cache`) is hidden from a normal `ls`. Programs keep their settings in dotfiles so they don't clutter your listing. `ls -a` shows them.

Hidden is not the same as secret. It's only a naming habit: anyone who knows the name, or runs `ls -a`, can see it. That's also why attackers sometimes hide their tools in dotfiles, and why investigators always look with `-a`.

sections.heading: The long listing
text: `ls -l` prints one line per entry with extra columns. In this lab they are:
points: The type and permissions, like `-rw-r--r--`. The first character is `d` for a directory or `-` for a file. The rest says who may read (r), write (w) or run (x) it, covered in a later chapter.
The owner: which user the file belongs to.
The size in bytes.

text: Real `ls -l` output has a few more columns (the group, a date, a link count), and `ls -a` also lists two special entries, `.` and `..`, which you'll meet in chapter 2. The ideas are the same.

sections.heading: Moving around with cd
text: `cd` (change directory) moves your shell to another directory. Afterwards, everything you type is relative to the new place: `ls` lists it, `cat file` reads from it. Watch the prompt: the part before `$` changes to show where you are.
`cd` itself prints nothing when it works. Silence means success, which is normal for Linux commands.

sections.heading: Going back up
text: Every directory has a parent: the one it sits inside. `..` is a special name that always means the parent, so `cd ..` goes up one level. You can climb and descend in one move: `cd ../south` means go up one level, then into `south`.

sections.heading: Two kinds of path
text: There are two ways to write a path, and the difference is the first character.
points: An absolute path starts with `/`. It's the full address from the root of the tree, so it points at the same file no matter where you are. Example: `/etc/hostname`.

A relative path doesn't start with `/`. It's read starting from your working directory, so the same relative path can point at different files depending on where you stand. Example: `notes.txt` or `etc/hostname`.

sections.heading: Reading a file without moving

sections.heading: When to use which

sections.heading: Nobody memorizes every command
text: Linux has thousands of commands and each has many options. Experienced people look things up constantly; the skill is knowing where to look. Every Linux system ships with built-in documentation, and this lab has a compact version of it.

sections.heading: man: the manual
text: `man COMMAND` shows the manual page for a command. On a full Linux system a manual page is long: it opens in a viewer where you scroll with the arrow keys, search with `/`, and quit with `q`. In this lab, `man` prints a short summary of the syntax and the options this lab supports.

sections.heading: How to read a syntax line
text: Manuals describe commands with a small notation. Once you can read it, any manual makes sense:
points: Square brackets mean optional: `ls [-al] [path]` works with or without options and with or without a path.
Letters inside brackets are options you can pick: `[-al]` means you can use `-a`, `-l` or both.
Capital words are placeholders you replace: in `cat FILE`, you type a real filename instead of FILE.
Three dots mean you can repeat the item: `cat [file...]` takes as many files as you like.

sections.heading: help: the list of commands
text: `help` lists every command this lab supports with a one-line description, plus the special symbols you can use. `help COMMAND` shows just one. On a full Linux system, `help` describes commands built into the shell, and many programs also explain themselves when you run them with `--help`.

sections.heading: Try one option at a time
text: When a manual mentions an option you haven't used, try it on something harmless and look at what changes. Reading the manual for `ls` is exactly how you'd discover the option this mission needs.
